In [[geometry]], a '''cleaver''' of a [[triangle]] is a [[line segment]] that [[Bisection|bisect]]s the [[perimeter]] of the triangle and has one endpoint at the [[midpoint]] of one of the three sides. They are not to be confused with ''[[Splitter (geometry)|splitters]]'', which also bisect the perimeter, but with an endpoint on one of the triangle's vertices instead of its sides.

==Construction==
Each cleaver through the midpoint of one of the sides of a triangle is parallel to the [[angle bisector]]s at the opposite vertex of the triangle.<ref name=episodes/><ref name=avishalom/>

The '''broken chord theorem''' of [[Archimedes]] provides another construction of the cleaver. Suppose the triangle to be bisected is {{math|△''ABC''}}, and that one endpoint of the cleaver is the midpoint of side {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}}. Form the [[circumcircle]] of {{math|△''ABC''}} and let {{mvar|M}} be the midpoint of the arc of the circumcircle from {{mvar|A}} through {{mvar|C}} to {{mvar|B}}. Then the other endpoint of the cleaver is the closest point of the triangle to {{mvar|M}}, and can be found by dropping a perpendicular from {{mvar|M}} to the longer of the two sides {{mvar|{{overline|AC}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}}.<ref name=episodes>{{citation
 | last = Honsberger | first = Ross | author-link = Ross Honsberger
 | contribution = Chapter 1: Cleavers and Splitters
